out: Tell apart policies, standards, procedures and guidelines.
Choose the right document for a situation.
plain: A policy says what must happen: all staff must wear seatbelts. A standard gives measurable requirements: the seatbelt must meet this rating. A procedure gives the steps: buckle it this way. A guideline gives recommended advice: consider adjusting your seat first.
tech: Guidelines are recommended, not mandatory, and include benchmarks, advisories, implementation guides and reference architecture. Standards are mandatory and measurable, and include baselines, passwords, physical security, encryption and technical specifications such as a request for comments (RFC).

Procedures are step-by-step instructions, such as a standard operating procedure (SOP) or a runbook. Plans include business continuity and disaster recovery. Policies set high-level expectations, including bring your own device (BYOD), acceptable use policy (AUP), clean desk, information security, incident response, data classification and retention, access control, data disposal, vulnerability disclosure and privacy.
terms: Notices about risks and recommended actions.
Request for comments: a published internet technical specification.
Prepared approaches such as business continuity and disaster recovery.
A plan to keep the organization functioning.
Bring your own device: rules for personal devices.
A policy to keep sensitive material out of sight.
A policy setting the organization's overall approach.
A policy establishing how incidents are handled.
A policy on labeling and keeping data.
A policy on who gets access.
A policy for receiving flaw reports.
A policy on handling personal information.
eg: A policy requires strong encryption, a standard specifies AES-256, and a procedure shows how to enable it on laptops.
A clean desk policy keeps printed customer information from being left out overnight.

lessons.title: Governance documents: guidelines, standards, procedures, plans and policies
lessons.domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight
lessons.why: Security decisions must be written down and enforceable. Exam questions often test whether you can tell a policy from a standard or a procedure.
lessons.scenario: An administrator needs step-by-step instructions to rotate a server's certificate. Which document type should this be?
lessons.answer: A procedure, such as an SOP or runbook, since it gives specific steps.

product: Policies become product requirements. An organization's password standard or acceptable use policy may need settings, enforcement and reporting in your product. Knowing the difference between a policy, a standard and a procedure helps you ask the right person.

sec: Which of our policies directly constrain this feature?

out: Choose a treatment and maintain a risk register.
plain: Consider home insurance. You think about what you own, what could happen, how likely it is and what it would cost. Then you lock the doors, buy insurance, move out of the flood zone or simply accept the small risks.
tech: Risk identification includes asset identification and stakeholder ownership. Risk assessment uses scoring and categorization. Risk analysis considers impact, likelihood or probability, the owner, current mitigations, and whether the method is qualitative (categories like high or low) or quantitative (numbers).

A risk register records risks, owners, scores and treatments, and supports communication and regular reviews. Risk treatment options are transferring (such as insurance), accepting, avoiding (stopping the activity) and mitigating (reducing the risk).

Business-level considerations include a business impact analysis (BIA), which identifies critical functions and the effect of losing them; risk appetite, the amount of risk an organization will pursue; residual risk, which remains after controls; stakeholder involvement; management oversight; and regulatory and legal requirements.

Quantitative risk: single loss expectancy (SLE) is asset value multiplied by exposure factor. The annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) is how many times per year an event is expected. Annualized loss expectancy (ALE) is SLE multiplied by ARO.
terms: Assigning people to be responsible for risks.
Assigning a value to a risk.
Grouping risks by type or level.
Examining impact and likelihood in depth.
The person accountable for a risk.
Using categories compared with using numbers.
A record of risks and their treatment.
Sharing risk information with those who need it.
Shifting financial impact to another party.
Stopping the activity that creates the risk.
Reducing a risk's likelihood or impact.
Identifying critical functions and the effect of losing them.
How much risk an organization is willing to take.
The risk that remains after controls.
Including affected people in risk decisions.
Requirements arising from laws and contracts.
Single loss expectancy: the cost of one event.
Annualized loss expectancy: expected yearly cost.
Annualized rate of occurrence: expected events per year.
eg: A laptop worth 2,000 dollars with an exposure factor of 100% has an SLE of 2,000. If two are lost a year, the ALE is 4,000. A control costing 500 a year that halves losses saves more than it costs.
A company buys cyber insurance, which transfers some financial impact but does not remove the risk of reputational harm.

table.caption: Risk treatments
rows: Shift financial impact to someone else

walks.title: Calculate quantitative risk
steps: Asset value is 100,000 dollars, and exposure factor is 40%.
SLE equals 100,000 times 0.40, which is 40,000.
ARO is 0.5, meaning once every two years.
ALE equals 40,000 times 0.5, which is 20,000 a year.
Compare that figure with what the control would cost.

labs.title: Create a risk register
do: Create five risks for a small online shop.
Score impact and likelihood from 1 to 5 and multiply.
Choose a treatment and an owner for each.
Calculate SLE and ALE for one of them.
Note the residual risk after treatment.
labs.expect: A sorted register with owners, treatments and one worked quantitative example.
labs.explain: The register turns abstract concerns into decisions that someone owns.
pass: Each risk has a score, owner and treatment.
Your SLE and ALE arithmetic is correct.

a.w: Financial impact shifts to the insurer.
The likelihood of an attack is unchanged.

qs.s: SLE is 8,000 dollars and ARO is 3. What is the ALE?

a.w: ALE equals SLE multiplied by ARO.

qs.s: What is residual risk?

a.t: The risk that remains after controls are applied
The risk before any controls exist
A risk that has been transferred

qs.s: A company stops offering a feature because its risk cannot be justified. Which treatment is this?

a.w: Stopping the activity removes the risk.
No other party took it on.
The company did not keep the risk.
The feature was removed, rather than made safer.

qs.s: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: Amount of risk willing to be taken
qs.why: Memorize the formula: ALE equals SLE times ARO.

mistakes: Thinking transferring removes the risk altogether. Reputational harm stays.
Accepting a risk without documenting who accepted it.
sum: Identify, assess, analyze, treat and review.
cards: What is the ALE formula?
ALE equals SLE multiplied by ARO.
Name the four risk treatments.
Transfer, accept, avoid, mitigate.
lessons.title: Risk management
lessons.domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight
lessons.why: Security is mostly about deciding which risks matter and what to do about them, with limited money and time.
lessons.scenario: A server costing 50,000 dollars would lose 20% of its value in a flood, and floods are expected once every ten years. What is the ALE?
lessons.answer: SLE is 50,000 times 0.2, which is 10,000. ARO is 0.1. ALE is 10,000 times 0.1, which is 1,000 dollars a year.

product: Risk management is how a team decides whether to ship. A feature with a known weakness might be accepted, mitigated or held back, and those decisions need to be recorded by someone with authority. Security requirements written during discovery are far cheaper than findings written after launch.

eng: What would it cost to reduce this risk now, compared with later?
sec: How do we score risk here, and who can accept it?
prod: What is the cost of delaying this release?

ex.title: Write security requirements during discovery
ex.scenario: Your team is starting discovery on bulk-invite for workspaces: admins upload a CSV to invite thousands of users, and invitations can grant any role.
ex.problem: Security review usually happens just before launch, when changes are expensive and contentious.
tasks: Identify the assets, actors and likely misuse.
Write a security requirements document with testable requirements.
Create a short risk register with likelihood, impact, treatment and owner.
List questions for engineering, security and product.
constraints: CSV contents are untrusted and may contain invalid or malicious values.
Requirements must be testable, not general wishes such as "be secure".
Designers propose treatments, while risk acceptance belongs to the authorized owner.
needs: Security staff need enough context to review.
Product managers need the trade-offs to plan a release.
ex.deliver: A one-page security requirements document and a risk register with at least five risks.

crit.t: Requirements are specific, testable and tied to the constraints.
Risks include misuse by authorized users as well as outside attackers.
The document can be read and used by non-security colleagues.
Each risk has a treatment and a named owner, with acceptance left to the authorized person.

seniors: Introducing security questions in discovery is one of the most valuable things a designer can do.
Your risk register supports the decision, and accountability stays with the risk owner.

cq.s: Which is the best security requirement for bulk invite?

a.t: Invited roles can't exceed the role of the inviting admin
a.w: It is specific, testable and limits privilege escalation.

a.t: The bulk invitation feature must be secure and trustworthy
a.w: This can't be tested or built against.

a.t: The team should think carefully about security for invitations
a.w: This is an intention and doesn't describe any behaviour.

a.t: Invitations should follow general industry best practices always
a.w: It is too vague to verify.

out: Follow a vendor from selection through monitoring.
plain: Hiring a vendor is like hiring a contractor to work inside your home. You get quotes, check references, sign a contract that spells out the work and keep an eye on the job.
tech: Vendor selection uses a request for proposal (RFP), request for information (RFI), request for quote (RFQ) and expression of interest (EOI). Due diligence evaluates a vendor before signing. Conflict of interest occurs when someone's personal interests could influence the decision.

Agreement types: a service-level agreement (SLA) defines measurable service commitments, and a service-level objective (SLO) is a specific target within it. A memorandum of understanding (MOU) records a general, usually non-binding, intent. A memorandum of agreement (MOA) is more specific about responsibilities. A non-disclosure agreement (NDA) protects confidential information. A master services agreement (MSA) sets general terms for future work. A statement of work (SOW) details specific deliverables.

Vendor monitoring includes right to audit, service-level monitoring, a vendor registry, vendor assessment, compliance attestation and penetration testing. Limitations and constraints include staffing limitations, resource availability, environment, legal and regulatory factors, geography/jurisdiction, financial/return on investment (ROI), vendor lock-in and assurance mechanisms. Rules of engagement define what testers may and may not do.
terms: A personal interest that could affect a decision.
Service-level objective: a specific service target.
Memorandum of understanding: a general statement of intent.
Memorandum of agreement: more specific responsibilities.
Master services agreement: general terms for future work.
A contractual right to examine a vendor.
A statement that a vendor meets requirements.
Not having enough people to oversee vendors.
The time, tools and budget available.
The technical or physical setting that limits testing.
Laws and regulations that constrain options.
Evidence such as audit reports and certifications.
What a tester is allowed to do.
eg: An MSA sets the general terms, and each project gets its own SOW.
A contract includes the right to audit, so a customer can verify that security promises are being kept.

table.caption: Selection documents
rows: Request pricing for a defined need

walks.title: Onboard a new SaaS vendor
steps: Use an RFP to compare options.
Run due diligence and review security attestations.
Sign an MSA and SLA, with data handling terms and right to audit.
Add it to the vendor registry and assign an owner.
Monitor service levels and reassess periodically.

labs.title: Conduct a vendor assessment

Note its certifications, data location and breach notification commitments.
Score it across five questions you write yourself.
List what you could not find and would need to ask.

labs.explain: Marketing claims differ from evidence. Noting what is missing is as valuable as what is present.

You listed at least two follow-up questions.

qs.s: Which document protects confidential information shared between parties?
Match each to its purpose.
qs.why: These agreements operate at different levels of specificity.

qs.s: Which contract clause allows a customer to examine a vendor's controls?

a.w: This is a constraint, not a clause.
This is an early purchasing document.

a.t: Rules of engagement, including scope and authorization
a.w: Testing without these can be illegal or harmful.
This is not the primary concern.

a.t: Nothing, if the tester is experienced

mistakes: Treating a vendor's marketing as evidence.
cards: What is the difference between an MSA and a SOW?
An MSA sets general terms, and a SOW details specific work.
What does a rules of engagement document define?
What testers are allowed to do, including scope and limits.
lessons.title: Third-party risk
lessons.domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight
lessons.why: Your suppliers' weaknesses become yours. A contract signed without due diligence can move risk into your organization unnoticed.
lessons.scenario: A company wants a document that details the exact tasks and deliverables a consultant will produce for a single project, under an existing general agreement. Which document fits?
lessons.answer: A statement of work (SOW), which sits under the master services agreement (MSA).

product: Vendor risk workflows are usually spreadsheets and email chains, and customers evaluating your product go through the same process in reverse. A trust center that shares certifications and answers on request is a product experience, and so is the internal tool that decides whether a new vendor gets customer data.

eng: Which vendors currently process customer data, and for what?
sec: What evidence do we require from a vendor, and how often is it refreshed?
prod: Which sales deals have been slowed by security questionnaires?

ex.title: Design a vendor security review workflow
ex.scenario: A growing company wants to replace its emailed spreadsheet process for reviewing software vendors. Any employee can currently sign up for a tool with company data.
ex.problem: Nobody knows which vendors hold what data, reviews are slow, and approved vendors are never checked again.
tasks: Design intake that asks a requester about data and access in plain language.
Design risk tiering that decides how deep the review goes.
Design the evidence and contract checklist, including the right to audit.
constraints: A vendor's assurance documents can be out of date or limited in scope.
Offboarding must include return or deletion of data.
Review effort must match risk, or staff will bypass it.
needs: Employees need a quick answer on low-risk tools.
Security and legal staff need one source of truth.
Leaders need to see overall vendor exposure.
ex.deliver: An intake and tiering flow, a review dashboard and a vendor life cycle diagram.

crit.t: Evidence, contract terms and offboarding are covered.
The design considers shadow IT, stale assessments and fourth parties.
A requester with no security background can finish the intake.
The process is tuned so that the secure path is also the easy path.

seniors: If the approved route is slow, people will avoid it, so treat turnaround time as a security measure.
Legal owns contract language, so design the hand-off and leave the wording to them.

cq.s: A vendor shares a SOC 2 report from two years ago. What should the workflow prompt?

a.t: Request a current report and check that its scope fits
a.w: Assurance can go stale, and it may not cover the service you use.

a.t: Accept it, because a SOC 2 report never loses its value
a.w: Reports describe a period and must be kept up to date.

a.t: Reject every vendor that has ever shared an older report
a.w: This is excessive, because a current report may simply exist.

a.t: Treat the report as proof that the vendor cannot be breached
a.w: No report can provide that guarantee.

out: Explain privacy rights and legal holds.
plain: Compliance is like following the rules of the road. You learn them, there are checks and there are penalties. Privacy law gives people rights over information about them, such as asking for corrections.
tech: Compliance training covers data handling, anti-money laundering/counter-terrorism financing (AML/CTF) and anti-bribery. Compliance monitoring uses attestations (formal statements that requirements are met) and acknowledgements (recording that someone has read and accepted something). Consequences of non-compliance include reputational damage, financial penalties, legal action, contractual breach, sanctions and loss of license.

Privacy concepts include the right to be forgotten (erasure), opt-in or opt-out consent choices, data correction, processing restrictions, processing prevention, the difference between controller vs. processor, and ownership of data. GDPR gives broad rights to individuals in the EU. In Canada, PIPEDA governs private-sector personal information in commercial activity federally, and some provinces, such as British Columbia, Alberta and Quebec, have their own substantially similar laws. FINTRAC is Canada's AML regulator.

Legal compliance covers a legal hold, which suspends normal deletion when litigation is reasonably expected; legal orders such as subpoenas or warrants; and data retention requirements, which set minimum or maximum retention periods.
terms: Checking whether requirements are being met.
Formal statements that requirements are met.
Records that someone read and accepted something.
A person's right to have data erased.
Choosing to give or withdraw consent.
A person's right to fix inaccurate data.
Limits on how data may be used.
The party deciding purposes compared with the party acting on instructions.
Who holds rights in the data.
Formal demands from courts or authorities.
Rules for how long data must be kept.
eg: A company receiving a deletion request must also check whether a legal hold requires keeping that data.
A Canadian retailer collecting customer data must follow PIPEDA or a substantially similar provincial law.

walks.title: Handle a deletion request
steps: Verify the person's identity.
Find where their data is stored, including backups and processors.
Check for legal holds or retention requirements.
Delete what can be deleted, and record the action.
Respond within the required time.

labs.title: Map privacy rights
do: Read the OPC summary of PIPEDA's fair information principles.
Read the European Commission's data protection overview.
Compare the two on consent, access and erasure in a small table.
Note one way a retention requirement could conflict with an erasure request.
labs.expect: A comparison table and a stated conflict.
labs.explain: Regulations differ, and real systems must be built to handle conflicting obligations.

qs.s: What does a legal hold do?

a.t: Suspends normal deletion of relevant data

a.w: It is not an encryption mechanism.

qs.s: A person asks an organization to delete their personal data. Which right is this?
Employees sign a form stating that they read the policy. What is this?

a.w: This comes from a court or authority.

qs.s: Which are consequences of non-compliance? Choose two.

a.w: An organization can lose the right to operate.

mistakes: Confusing a legal hold with data retention rules.
Assuming deletion is always required and always possible.
sum: Non-compliance has many kinds of consequence.
Privacy rights must be balanced with legal duties.
cards: What is a legal hold?
An instruction to preserve relevant data, suspending normal deletion.
What is an attestation?
A formal statement that requirements are met.
lessons.title: Security compliance and privacy
lessons.domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight
lessons.why: Compliance failures bring fines, lost licenses and lost trust. Privacy obligations affect how systems must be built, including what they can delete.
lessons.scenario: A customer asks to have their data deleted, but the company has been told to preserve records relating to a lawsuit that includes that customer. What takes priority?
lessons.answer: The legal hold. Relevant data must be preserved. The company should explain the limitation, and handle the deletion when the hold ends, under legal guidance.

product: Privacy is directly experienced in products: consent prompts, cookie banners, settings, notices and retention choices. Dark patterns can turn consent into coercion. Good privacy design gives people real choices and respects the difference between controllers and processors and between regional obligations.

eng: Can consent be enforced technically, so data use actually stops?
sec: Which data flows change depending on region?
prod: Which privacy regulations apply, and who confirms that?

ex.title: Design privacy controls and consent
ex.scenario: A health and wellness app wants to use member data to personalize content and share aggregated insights with partners. It operates in Canada and the EU.
ex.problem: Currently one checkbox at sign-up covers everything, and members can't later change their choices or see what is being shared.
tasks: Separate necessary processing from optional uses.
Design a privacy center: choices, history, access, deletion.
Show what changes when consent is withdrawn.
constraints: Withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it, and must really stop the processing.
Health data has stricter handling obligations in many jurisdictions.
Regional legal requirements must be confirmed by privacy counsel.
needs: Members need to understand trade-offs in plain language.
The business needs valid, recorded consent.
Privacy officers need proof of what was agreed and when.
ex.deliver: A layered consent flow, a privacy center and a data-use map.

crit.t: Consent is granular, withdrawable and technically enforced.
The design avoids dark patterns and considers re-identification from aggregated data.
Choices are written in plain language at the point of decision.
The design makes clear which assumptions need legal confirmation.

seniors: Privacy is more than compliance, so ask whether a person would be surprised by this data use.
Legal review confirms requirements, and your job is making the choice real for users.

cq.s: Which pattern best supports meaningful consent?

a.t: Separate, unticked choices and an equally easy decline
a.w: People make specific choices without being steered.

a.t: A single pre-ticked box that covers every possible data use
a.w: Pre-ticked, bundled consent doesn't reflect a real choice.

a.t: A large Accept button beside a tiny hidden decline link
a.w: This steers people, which makes it a dark pattern.

a.t: Consent wording placed only inside the full terms of service
a.w: People can't make a specific choice from buried terms.

out: Plan an audit, including data gathering and scoping.
Distinguish penetration test types and passive and active reconnaissance.
Use MITRE ATT&CK, the Cyber Kill Chain and the Diamond Model.
plain: An audit is a health check by someone looking at your records. A penetration test is hiring a friendly burglar to try the doors. Known environment means the burglar has floor plans. Unknown environment means they have none.
tech: Data gathering uses sampling, questionnaires/surveys, interviews and assertion, which is a claim to be tested. Reference sources include MITRE ATT&CK, a knowledge base of real attacker techniques; the Cyber Kill Chain, which describes the stages of an intrusion; and the Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis, which relates adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim. Scoping uses an audit charter, which sets authority and purpose, and frequency.

Engagement types include gap analysis; internal work by compliance staff, the audit committee and self-assessments; external work, including examinations, assessments, regulatory reviews and independent third-party audits; and benchmarking against peers or standards.

Penetration testing can be known environment (full details), unknown environment (no details) or partially known environment. It may be physical, offensive (attacking), defensive (defending) or integrated (both sides working together, often called purple teaming). Reconnaissance can be passive, which avoids touching the target, such as public records, or active, which interacts with the target, such as scanning.

Frameworks and standards include industry-based standards such as PCI DSS, international standards such as ISO/IEC 27001, and region-specific standards such as GDPR requirements. Functional testing checks that a control works as designed, and behavioral testing checks how people or systems actually act.
terms: Examining a subset to draw conclusions.
Written questions used to collect information.
Direct conversations used to gather evidence.
A knowledge base of attacker tactics and techniques.
A model of the stages of an intrusion.
A model linking adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim.
A document setting the authority and purpose of auditing.
Comparing the current state with a target.
Internal work to confirm requirements are met.
A governing group that oversees audits.
Reviews carried out by the organization itself.
Audits by an outside, impartial party.
Testing with full knowledge of the target.
Offensive and defensive teams working together.
Reconnaissance that does not touch the target.
Reconnaissance that interacts with the target.
Checking that a control works as designed.
Checking how people or systems really act.
eg: A SOC maps its detections to MITRE ATT&CK techniques and finds it has none for credential dumping.
Reading a company's job adverts to learn its technologies is passive reconnaissance. Scanning its servers is active.

walks.title: Scope a penetration test
steps: Obtain written authorization.
Define the systems in and out of scope.
Choose known, partially known or unknown environment.
Agree rules of engagement, timing and emergency contacts.
Report findings, then verify that they were fixed.

Find the ATT&CK tactic and technique for each.

qs.s: Searching public records about a target, without touching its systems, is which?

a.w: There is no interaction with the target.
Active reconnaissance interacts with the target.
This is practice for incident response.

qs.s: Testers receive complete network diagrams and source code. Which is this?

a.w: This is one activity, not an engagement type.

qs.s: Match each framework to what it describes.
qs.why: They look at an intrusion from different angles.

a.w: It is carried out by an outside, impartial party.

a.t: A questionnaire filled in by the system's own administrator

a.w: This is about knowledge of the target.
This is a data gathering method.

Starting any test without written authorization.
sum: Pen tests differ in knowledge and approach.
ATT&CK, Kill Chain and the Diamond Model describe attacks differently.
cards: Passive or active: is port scanning a target passive?
No. Scanning interacts with the target, so it is active.
What are the four elements of the Diamond Model?
Adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim.
lessons.title: Audits, assessments and penetration testing
lessons.domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight
lessons.why: Audits confirm that controls actually work. Knowing the type of engagement tells you who does what, and with what independence.
lessons.scenario: A company hires testers and gives them no information about its systems. What type of test is this?
lessons.answer: An unknown environment penetration test. They begin with nothing, simulating an outside attacker's starting point.

product: Audits and penetration tests produce work for product teams and evidence requests that products can make easier. Admin screens that export access reviews and configuration history turn an audit scramble into a routine task.

sec: What evidence do auditors repeatedly ask us for?

out: Choose training types and delivery mechanisms.
Build a topic plan including BEC and operational security.
plain: Awareness training is like fire drills. A single talk is forgotten. Regular, specific practice, followed by feedback, means that people know what to do when it matters.
tech: Types of training include initial/onboarding when someone joins, ongoing, targeted (for a role or risk) and corrective (following a mistake). Delivery mechanisms include a learning management system (LMS), self-service portals, one-to-one and one-to-many sessions.

Reporting and monitoring of effectiveness uses metrics (such as phishing report rates), managerial reports and personnel behavior risk scoring, which should be used carefully and fairly. Common training topics include social engineering, emerging security topics, password and credential management, remote work/teleworking/hybrid, BYOD, business email compromise (BEC), removable media and cables, situational awareness and operational security.
terms: Training for a specific role or risk.
Sites where staff access training themselves.
Measures such as phishing report rates.
Rating risk based on observed behaviour.
USB devices and charging cables that may be malicious.
Noticing what is happening around you.
eg: After a phishing simulation, those who clicked get short corrective training, and those who report are thanked. Reporting rate is tracked, more than click rate alone.
A finance team receives targeted training on BEC, including a call-back step for any payment change.

steps: Identify the top human risks.
Decide on training type and delivery for each.
Set measures, such as time to report phishing.
Run the training and communicate results to managers.
Adjust it according to results.

Draft a short message that tells staff how to report a suspicious email.
Note how you would keep scoring fair and proportionate.

labs.explain: The aim is changed behaviour, and a culture in which reporting is encouraged, not embarrassment.

lessons.title: Security awareness
lessons.domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight
lessons.why: People are both a common target and an early warning system. Good awareness programs change behaviour, and that is what should be measured.
lessons.scenario: The finance team was caught by a fake invoice email from a supplier's compromised account. Which training is most appropriate?
lessons.answer: Targeted training on business email compromise, including verifying payment changes through a known phone number.

product: Security awareness is partly a product problem. Clear warnings, easy phishing-report buttons and well-timed advice work better than annual training alone. Punishing people who click can discourage the reporting that the organization most needs.

eng: Can we surface security tips in context without being noisy?
sec: How do people report suspicious activity today?
prod: How do we measure whether behaviour actually changes?

design.noex: The phishing exercise in Week 6 applies this. Awareness is a shared organizational program and not a design task on its own.
